A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FoA research, with matching algorithms and identifiable corresponding experiments. The text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. v1 ends with references; v2's Appendices A-C were included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original FoA and ToT experiments on Game of 24 and Mini Crosswords using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, including performance, costs, and confidence intervals in Tables 1-4.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds WebShop, Llama evaluations, broader baseline comparisons, and component ablations in the main text and Appendix C.

M1.justification: The mutation/selection cycle, enforced mutation, sudden-death resampling, and discounted backtracking remain unchanged; Algorithms 1-3 move to Appendix B. Appendix C newly documents caching, batching, and selected resampling settings, including linear-filtered resampling, without establishing that the earlier implementation used a different procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds WebShop alongside the retained Game of 24 and Mini Crosswords datasets. This substantially extends evaluation from self-contained puzzles to sequential decision-making in a simulated shopping environment, requiring navigation, product selection, and purchase.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares against ToT, with literature-sourced IO and CoT reference scores for GPT-4 Game of 24. v2 adds evaluated CoT-SC, AoT, GoT, and RAFA comparisons for Game of 24, and IO, CoT, CoT-SC, and GoT for Crosswords. WebShop adds Act, ReAct, Reflexion, LASER, and LATS. RAFA is evaluated with GPT-3.5 and Llama-11B, not the configurations marked DNR.

E3.justification: The original puzzle splits and metrics are retained. v2 adds Llama3.2-11B/90B evaluation settings, a WebShop design with 50 test and 15 validation tasks, and a new budget-controlled experiment in Section 5 that allocates $5 per method and measures success across multiple trials. These extend the evaluation design substantially.

E4.justification: v1 describes hyperparameter searches and reports selected configurations but has no component ablations. v2 adds removal or alteration studies for selection, resampling, backtracking, caching, and batching across tasks (Figures 6, 11, and 12), explicit hyperparameter sensitivity plots (Figures 8-10), and model-size and budget analyses.

E5.justification: v1 displays benchmark confidence intervals, specifies bootstrap intervals for GPT-4 Game of 24, and qualifies its nonsignificant accuracy advantage. v2 removes those intervals and qualifications. It retains the stated one-run GPT-4/five-run GPT-3.5 practice and extends five-run reporting to other models, but the promised standard errors are absent from Tables 6-8. New sensitivity plots contain error bars whose meaning is not specified.

E6.justification: Many original FoA values remain unchanged, including GPT-4 Game of 24 at 76% and $62.93 and Crosswords at 46% and $12.938. The reported GPT-4 ToT Game of 24 score changes from 75% to 74%, and the additional GPT-3.5 FoA operating points disappear. Substantial new results cover baselines, Llama models, ablations, and WebShop, where FoA reports 75.6 average score versus LATS's 66.1.

T1.justification: The state and transition definitions, solution/terminal-state assumptions, resampling formulas, and discounted-backtracking formulation are retained. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive formal analysis.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes efficiency and accuracy relative to ToT on two puzzles. v2 broadens the central claims to superiority over multiple SOTA methods, approximately 5% better quality at 40% of their cost, the best trade-off at all price points, and FoA enabling Llama-11B to surpass the standalone 90B model. These materially expand the claimed scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving fleet diversity, noisy historical value estimates, and inconsistent repeated evaluations, plus a fixed-fleet-size limitation and the qualification that ToT might catch up at higher budgets. It removes v1's warning about failing to reproduce published GPT-4 Crossword results and its explicit caveat about backtracking through irreversible actions.

D1.justification: v1 mainly identifies reused ToT prompts and broad hyperparameter categories. v2 supplies seven prompt templates, model checkpoints, API providers, token prices, generation settings, tuning plots and selected configurations, and caching/batching details in Appendix C. It also supplies a FoA code-access URL. These substantially improve implementation and reproduction documentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning through discussions of AoT, meta-prompting, BoT, Reflexion, RAFA, RAP, LATS, and other methods, organized into reasoning, refinement, and search categories. A new key-differences discussion emphasizes cost-quality control, and Section 7.2 adds a first-to-analyze-this-trade-off claim. The older general agent-framework discussion largely moves to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around cost-quality trade-offs. Experiments are reorganized with GPT-4 puzzle results in the main text and additional models in Appendix C; separate model-analysis, ablation, discussion, and limitations sections are introduced. Algorithms and substantial background move to appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the framework comparison, and separates the retained FoA schematic into Figure 3. It adds budget/model-size plots, ablation panels, tuning curves, and an illustrative trajectory. Benchmark tables are expanded and reorganized, with colored rankings in the main text and model-grouped appendix tables; pseudocode is relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow comparative evidence and sparse reproduction details through broader baselines, interactive WebShop evaluation, component ablations, and detailed Appendix C documentation. These strengthen the assessment of FoA's applicability and mechanisms. Material regressions remain: benchmark confidence intervals disappear, and Section 4.1 claims a 25% cost reduction where Table 1 implies about 16%. Nevertheless, the gains in validation and reproducibility constitute a substantial overall improvement.
